entries.fe9b658dba2473ebcb723a1dc715078bc8bb398a: <div sID="gen8295" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="24" osisID="2Chr.24" sID="2Chr.24"/> <div eID="gen8295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8296" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8297" type="x-p"/> We have here the history of the reign of Joash, the progress of which, and especially its termination, were not of a piece with its beginning, nor shone with so much lustre. How wonderfully he was preserved for the throne, and placed in it, we read before; now here we are told how he began in the spirit, but ended in the flesh. I. In the beginning of his time, while Jehoiada lived, he did well; particularly, he took care to put the temple in good repair, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.1-2Chr.24.14">ver. 1-14</reference>. II. In the latter end of his time, after Jehoiada's death, he apostatized from God, and his apostasy was his ruin. 1. He set up the worship of Baal again (<reference osisRef="2Chr.24.15-2Chr.24.18">ver. 15-18</reference>), though warned to the contrary, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.19">ver. 19</reference>. 2. He put Zechariah the prophet to death because he reproved him for what he had done, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.20-2Chr.24.22">ver. 20-22</reference>. 3. The judgments of God came upon him for it. The Syrians invaded him, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.23-2Chr.24.24">ver. 23, 24</reference>. He was struck with sore diseases; his own servants conspired against him and slew him; and, as a mark of infamy upon him, he was not buried in the burying-place of the kings, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.25-2Chr.24.27">ver. 25-27</reference>.
entries.bea681f814f43d26f2dc16013a57b450f8273e94: <div eID="gen8297" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8296" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Temple Repaired. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 855.)</title> <div sID="gen8298" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Joash <hi type="italic">was</hi> seven years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother's name also <hi type="italic">was</hi> Zibiah of Beer-sheba. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Joash did <hi type="italic">that which was</hi> right in the sight of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> all the days of Jehoiada the priest. <hi type="super">3</hi> And Jehoiada took for him two wives; and he begat sons and daughters. <hi type="super">4</hi> And it came to pass after this, <hi type="italic">that</hi> Joash was minded to repair the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">5</hi> And he gathered together the priests and the Levites, and said to them, Go out unto the cities of Judah, and gather of all Israel money to repair the house of your God from year to year, and see that ye hasten the matter. Howbeit the Levites hastened <hi type="italic">it</hi> not. <hi type="super">6</hi> And the king called for Jehoiada the chief, and said unto him, Why hast thou not required of the Levites to bring in out of Judah and out of Jerusalem the collection, <hi type="italic">according to the commandment</hi> of Moses the servant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and of the congregation of Israel, for the tabernacle of witness? <hi type="super">7</hi> For the sons of Athaliah, that wicked woman, had broken up the house of God; and also all the dedicated things of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> did they bestow upon Baalim. <hi type="super">8</hi> And at the king's commandment they made a chest, and set it without at the gate of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">9</hi> And they made a proclamation through Judah and Jerusalem, to bring in to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> the collection <hi type="italic">that</hi> Moses the servant of God <hi type="italic">laid</hi> upon Israel in the wilderness. <hi type="super">10</hi> And all the princes and all the people rejoiced, and brought in, and cast into the chest, until they had made an end. <hi type="super">11</hi> Now it came to pass, that at what time the chest was brought unto the king's office by the hand of the Levites, and when they saw that <hi type="italic">there was</hi> much money, the king's scribe and the high priest's officer came and emptied the chest, and took it, and carried it to his place again. Thus they did day by day, and gathered money in abundance. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the king and Jehoiada gave it to such as did the work of the service of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and hired masons and carpenters to repair the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and also such as wrought iron and brass to mend the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">13</hi> So the workmen wrought, and the work was perfected by them, and they set the house of God in his state, and strengthened it. <hi type="super">14</hi> And when they had finished <hi type="italic">it,</hi> they brought the rest of the money before the king and Jehoiada, whereof were made vessels for the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">even</hi> vessels to minister, and to offer <hi type="italic">withal,</hi> and spoons, and vessels of gold and silver. And they offered burnt offerings in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> continually all the days of Jehoiada. <div eID="gen8298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8299" type="x-p"/> This account of Joash's good beginnings we had as it stands here <reference osisRef="2Kgs.12.1-2Kgs.12.21">2 Kings xii. 1</reference>, &c., though the latter part of this chapter, concerning his apostasy, we had little of there. What is good in men we should take all occasions to speak of and often repeat it; what is evil we should make mention of but sparingly, and no more than is needful. We shall here only observe, 1. That it is a happy thing for young people, when they are setting out in the world, to be under the direction of those that are wise and good and faithful to them, as Joash was under the influence of Jehoiada, during whose time he <hi type="italic">did that which was right.</hi> Let those that are young reckon it a blessing to them, and not a burden and check upon them, to have those with them that will caution them against that which is evil and advise and quicken them to that which is good; and let them reckon it not a mark of weakness and subjection, but of wisdom and discretion, to hearken to such. He that will not be counselled cannot be helped. It is especially prudent for young people to take advice in their marriages, as Joash did, who left it to his guardian to choose him his wives, because Jezebel and Athaliah had been such plagues, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.3">v. 3</reference>. This is a turn of life which often proves either the making or marring of young people, and therefore should be attended to with great care. 2. Men may go far in the external performances of religion, and keep long to them, merely by the power of their education and the influence of their friends, who yet have no hearty affection for divine things nor any inward relish of them. Foreign inducements may push men on to that which is good who are not actuated by a living principle of grace in their hearts. 3. In the outward expressions of devotion it is possible that those who have only the form of godliness may out-strip those who have the power of it. Joash is more solicitous and more zealous about the repair of the temple than Jehoiada himself, whom he reproves for his remissness in that matter, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.6">v. 6</reference>. It is easier to build temples than to be temples to God. 4. The repairing of churches is a good work, which all in their places should promote, for the decency and conveniency of religious assemblies. The learned tell us that in the Christian church, anciently, part of the tithes were applied that way. 5. Many a good work would be done that now lies undone if there were but a few active men to stir in it and to put it forward. When Joash found the money did not come in as he expected in one way he tried another way, and that answered the intention. Many have honesty enough to follow that have not zeal enough to lead in that which is good. The throwing of money into a chest, through a hole in the lid of it, was a way that had not been used before, and perhaps the very novelty of the thing made it a successful expedient for the raising of money; a great deal was thrown in and with a great deal of cheerfulness: they all rejoiced, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.10">v. 10</reference>. An invention to please people's humour may sometimes bring them to their duty. Wisdom herein is profitable to direct. 6. Faithfulness is the greatest praise and will be the greatest comfort of those that are entrusted with public treasure or employed in public business. The king and Jehoiada faithfully paid the money to the workmen, who faithfully did the work, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.12-2Chr.24.13">v. 12, 13</reference>.
entries.10ba02bc8e1f037af25d2d5ce5ff4a96be9c8f5e: <div eID="gen8299" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Joash Slain by His Servants. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 845.)</title> <div sID="gen8300" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> But Jehoiada waxed old, and was full of days when he died; a hundred and thirty years old <hi type="italic">was he</hi> when he died. <hi type="super">16</hi> And they buried him in the city of David among the kings, because he had done good in Israel, both toward God, and toward his house. <hi type="super">17</hi> Now after the death of Jehoiada came the princes of Judah, and made obeisance to the king. Then the king hearkened unto them. <hi type="super">18</hi> And they left the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of their fathers, and served groves and idols: and wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem for this their trespass. <hi type="super">19</hi> Yet he sent prophets to them, to bring them again unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and they testified against them: but they would not give ear. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the Spirit of God came upon Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, which stood above the people, and said unto them, Thus saith God, Why transgress ye the commandments of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that ye cannot prosper? because ye have forsaken the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , he hath also forsaken you. <hi type="super">21</hi> And they conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">22</hi> Thus Joash the king remembered not the kindness which Jehoiada his father had done to him, but slew his son. And when he died, he said, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> look upon <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and require <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">23</hi> And it came to pass at the end of the year, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the host of Syria came up against him: and they came to Judah and Jerusalem, and destroyed all the princes of the people from among the people, and sent all the spoil of them unto the king of Damascus. <hi type="super">24</hi> For the army of the Syrians came with a small company of men, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> delivered a very great host into their hand, because they had forsaken the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of their fathers. So they executed judgment against Joash. <hi type="super">25</hi> And when they were departed from him, (for they left him in great diseases,) his own servants conspired against him for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest, and slew him on his bed, and he died: and they buried him in the city of David, but they buried him not in the sepulchres of the kings. <hi type="super">26</hi> And these are they that conspired against him; Zabad the son of Shimeath an Ammonitess, and Jehozabad the son of Shimrith a Moabitess. <hi type="super">27</hi> Now <hi type="italic">concerning</hi> his sons, and the greatness of the burdens <hi type="italic">laid</hi> upon him, and the repairing of the house of God, behold, they <hi type="italic">are</hi> written in the story of the book of the kings. And Amaziah his son reigned in his stead. <div eID="gen8300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8301" type="x-p"/> We have here a sad account of the degeneracy and apostasy of Joash. God had done great things for him; he had done something for God; but now he proved ungrateful to his God and false to the engagements he had laid himself under to him. <hi type="italic">How has the gold become dim, and the most fine gold changed!</hi> Here we find, <div eID="gen8301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8302" type="x-p"/> I. The occasions of his apostasy. When he did that which was right it was <hi type="italic">not with a perfect heart.</hi> He never was sincere, never acted from principle, but in compliance to Jehoiada, who had helped him to the crown, and because he had been protected in the temple and rose upon the ruins of idolatry; and therefore, when the wind turned, he turned with it. 1. His good counsellor left him, and was by death removed from him. It was a mercy to him and his kingdom that Jehoiada lived so long-130 years (<reference osisRef="2Chr.24.15">v. 15</reference>), by which it appears that he was born in Solomon's time, and had lived six entire reigns before this. It was an encouragement to him to go on in that good way which Jehoiada had trained him up in to see what honour was done to Jehoiada at his death: <hi type="italic">They buried him among the kings,</hi> with this honourable encomium (perhaps it was part of the inscription on his grave-stone), that <hi type="italic">he had done good in Israel.</hi> Judah is called <hi type="italic">Israel,</hi> because, the other tribes having revolted from God, they only were Israelites indeed. Note, It is the greatest honour to do good in our generations, and those who <hi type="italic">do that which is good shall have praise of the same.</hi> He had done good towards God; not that any man's goodness can extend unto him, but he had done good towards his house, in reviving the temple service, <reference osisRef="2Chr.23.8">ch. xxiii. 8</reference>. Note, Those do the greatest good to their country that lay out themselves in their places to promote religion. Well, Jehoiada finished his course with honour; but the little religion that Joash had was all buried in his grave, and, after his death, both king and kingdom miserably degenerated. See how much one head may sustain, and what a great judgment to any prince or people the death of godly, zealous, useful men is. See how necessary it is that, as our Saviour speaks, we <hi type="italic">have salt in ourselves,</hi> that we act in religion from an inward principle, which will carry us on through all changes. Then the loss of a parent, a minister, a friend, will not involve the loss of our religion. 2. Bad counsellors got about him, insinuated themselves into his affections, wheedled him, flattered him, <hi type="italic">made obeisance</hi> to him, and, instead of condoling, congratulated him upon the death of his old tutor, as his release from the discipline he had been so long under, unworthy a man, a king. They tell him he must be priest-ridden no longer, he is now discharged from <hi type="italic">grave lessons and restraints,</hi> he may do as he pleases: and (would you think it?) the princes of Judah were the men that were so industrious to debauch him, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.17">v. 17</reference>. His father and grandfather were corrupted by the house of Ahab, from whom no better could be expected. But that the princes of Judah should be seducers to their king was very sad. But those that incline to the <hi type="italic">counsels of the ungodly</hi> will never want ungodly counsellors. They <hi type="italic">made obeisance to the king,</hi> flattered him into an opinion of his absolute power, promised to stand by him in making his royal will and pleasure pass for a law, any divine precept or institution to the contrary in any wise notwithstanding. And he hearkened to them: their discourse pleased him, and was more agreeable than Jehoiada's dictates used to be. Princes and inferior people have been many a time thus flattered into their ruin by those who have promised them liberty and dignity, but who have really brought them into the greatest servitude and disgrace. <div eID="gen8302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8303" type="x-p"/> II. The apostasy itself: <hi type="italic">They left the house of God, and served groves and idols,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.18">v. 18</reference>. The princes, it is likely, had a request to the king, which they tell him they durst not offer while Jehoiada lived; but now they hope it will give no offence: it is that they may set up the groves and idols again which were thrown down in the beginning of his reign, for they hate to be always confined to the dull old-fashioned service of the temple. And he not only gave them leave to do it themselves, but he joined with them. The king and princes, who, a little while ago, were repairing the temple, now forsook the temple; those who had pulled down groves and idols now themselves served them. So inconstant a thing is man and so little confidence is to be put in him! <div eID="gen8303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8304" type="x-p"/> III. The aggravations of this apostasy and the additions of guilt to it. God <hi type="italic">sent prophets to them</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.24.19">v. 19</reference>) to reprove them for their wickedness, and to tell them what would be in the end thereof, and so <hi type="italic">to bring them again unto the Lord.</hi> It is the work of ministers to bring people, not to themselves, but to God—to bring those again to him who have gone a whoring from him. In the most degenerate times God <hi type="italic">left not himself without witness;</hi> though they had dealt very disingenuously with God, yet he sent prophets to them to convince and instruct them, and to assure them that they should find favour with him if yet they would return; for he would rather sinners should <hi type="italic">turn and live</hi> than <hi type="italic">go on and die,</hi> and those that perish shall be left inexcusable. The prophets did their part: <hi type="italic">they testified against them;</hi> but, few or none <hi type="italic">received their testimony.</hi> <div eID="gen8304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8305" type="x-p"/> 1. They slighted all the prophets; they would not give ear, were so strangely wedded to their idols that no reproofs, warnings, threatenings, nor any of the various methods which the prophets took to convince them would reclaim them. Few would hear them, fewer would heed them, but fewest of all would believe them or be governed by them. <div eID="gen8305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8306" type="x-p"/> 2. They slew one of the most eminent, <hi type="italic">Zechariah the son of Jehoiada,</hi> and perhaps others. Concerning him observe, <div eID="gen8306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8307" type="x-p"/> (1.) The message which he delivered to them in the name of God, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.20">v. 20</reference>. The people were assembled in the court of the temple (for they had not quite left it), probably on occasion of some solemn feast, when this Zechariah, being filled with the spirit of prophecy, and known (it is likely) to be a prophet, stood up in some of the desks that were in the court of the priests, and very plainly, but without any provoking language, told the people of their sin and what would be the consequences of it. He did not impeach any particular persons, nor predict any particular judgments, as sometimes the prophets did, but as inoffensively as possible reminded them of what was written in the law. Let them but look into their Bibles, and there they would find, [1.] The precept they broke: "<hi type="italic">You transgress the commandments of the Lord,</hi> you know you do so, in serving groves and idols: and why will you so offend God and wrong yourselves?" [2.] The penalty they incurred: "You know, if the word of God be true, you cannot prosper in this evil way; never expect to do ill and fare well. Nay, you find already that <hi type="italic">because you have forsaken the Lord he hath forsaken you,</hi> as he told you he would," <reference osisRef="Deut.29.25">Deut. xxix. 25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.31.16-Deut.31.17">xxxi. 16, 17</reference>. This is the work of ministers, by the word of God, as a lamp and a light, to expose the sin of men and expound the providences of God. <div eID="gen8307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8308" type="x-p"/> (2.) The barbarous treatment they gave him for his kindness and faithfulness in delivering this message to them, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.21">v. 21</reference>. By the conspiracy of the princes, or some of their party, and <hi type="italic">by the commandment of the king,</hi> who thought himself affronted by this fair warning, they stoned him to death immediately, not under colour of law, accusing him as a blasphemer, a traitor, or a false prophet, but in a popular tumult, <hi type="italic">in the court of the house of the Lord</hi>—as horrid a piece of wickedness as perhaps any we read of in all the history of the kings. The <hi type="italic">person</hi> was sacred—a priest, the <hi type="italic">place</hi> sacred—the court of the temple (the inner court, <hi type="italic">between the porch and the altar</hi>), the <hi type="italic">message</hi> yet more sacred, and we have reason to think that they knew it came from the spirit of prophecy. The reproof was just, the warning fair, both backed with scripture, and the delivery very gentle and tender; and yet so impudently and daringly do they defy God himself that nothing less than the blood of the prophet can satisfy their indignation at the prophecy. <hi type="italic">Be astonished, O heavens! at this,</hi> and <hi type="italic">tremble, O earth!</hi> that ever such villany should be committed by men, by Israelites, in contempt and violation of every thing that is just, honourable, and sacred—that a king, a king in covenant with God, should command the murder of one whom it was his office to protect and countenance! The Jews say there were seven transgressions in this; for they killed a priest, a prophet, a judge, they shed innocent blood, and polluted the court of the temple, the sabbath, and the day of expiation: for on that day, their tradition says, this happened. <div eID="gen8308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8309" type="x-p"/> (3.) The aggravation of this sin, that this Zechariah, who suffered martyrdom for his faithfulness to God and his country, was the son of Jehoiada, who had done so much good in Israel, and particularly had been as a father to Joash, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.22">v. 22</reference>. The affront done by it to God, and the contempt put on religion, are not so particularly taken notice of as the ingratitude there was in it to the memory of Jehoiada. He remembered not the kindness of the father, but slew the son for doing his duty, and what the father would have done if he had been there. Call a man ungrateful, and you can call him no worse. <div eID="gen8309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8310" type="x-p"/> (4.) The dying martyr's prophetic imprecation of vengeance upon his murderers: <hi type="italic">The Lord look upon it, and require it!</hi> This came not from a spirit of revenge, but a spirit of prophecy: <hi type="italic">He will require it.</hi> This would be the continual cry of the blood they shed, as Abel's blood cried against Cain: "Let the God to whom vengeance belongs demand blood for blood. He will do it, for he is righteous." This precious blood was quickly reckoned for in the judgments that came upon this apostate prince; it came into the account afterwards in the destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans—their misusing the prophets was that which brought upon them ruin without remedy (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.16">ch. xxxvi. 16</reference>); nay, our Saviour makes the persecutors of him and his gospel answerable for the blood of this Zechariah; so loud, so long, does the blood of the martyrs cry. See <reference osisRef="Matt.23.35">Matt. xxiii. 35</reference>. Such as this is the cry of the souls under the altar (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.10">Rev. vi. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">How long ere thou avenge our blood?</hi> For it shall not always go unrevenged. <div eID="gen8310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8311" type="x-p"/> IV. The judgments of God which came upon Joash for this aggravated wickedness of his. 1. A small army of Syrians made themselves masters of Jerusalem, destroyed the princes, plundered the city, and sent the spoil of it to Damascus, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.23-2Chr.24.24">v. 23, 24</reference>. God's people, while they kept in with God, had often been conquerors when the enemy had the advantage of the greater number; but now, on the contrary, an inconsiderable handful of Syrians routed a <hi type="italic">very great host of Israelites, because they had forsaken the Lord God of their fathers,</hi> and then they were not only put upon the level with their enemies, but opposed them with the utmost disadvantage; for their God not only departed from them, but <hi type="italic">turned to be their enemy and fought against them.</hi> The Syrians were employed as instruments in God's hand to <hi type="italic">execute judgments against Joash,</hi> though they little thought so, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.6-Isa.10.7">Isa. x. 6, 7</reference>, and see <reference osisRef="Deut.32.30">Deut. xxxii. 30</reference>. 2. God smote him with great diseases, of body, or mind, or both, either like his grandfather (<reference osisRef="2Chr.21.18">ch. xxi. 18</reference>), or, like Saul, an evil spirit from God troubling him. While he was plagued with the Syrians he thought that, if he could but get clear of them, he should do well enough. But, before they departed from him, God smote him with diseases. If vengeance pursue men, the end of one trouble will but be the beginning of another. 3. His own servants conspired against him. Perhaps he began to hope his disease would be cured—he was but a middle-aged man and might recover it; but <hi type="italic">he that cometh up out of the pit shall fall into the snare.</hi> When he thought he should escape death by sickness he met it by the sword. They slew him in his bed <hi type="italic">for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada,</hi> by which it should seem that he did not only slay Zechariah, but others of the sons of Jehoiada for his sake. Perhaps those that slew him <hi type="italic">intended</hi> to take vengeance for that blood; but, whether they did or not, this was what God intended in permitting them to slay him. Those that drink the blood of the saints shall have their own blood given them to drink, for they are worthy. The regicides are here named (<reference osisRef="2Chr.24.26">v. 26</reference>), and it is observable that the mothers of them both were foreigners, one an Ammonitess and the other a Moabitess. The idolatrous kings, it is likely, countenanced those marriages which the law prohibited for the prevention of idolatry; and see how they resulted in their own destruction. 4. His people would not bury him in the sepulchres of the kings because he had stained his honour by his mal-administration. <hi type="italic">Let him not be written with the righteous,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.69.28">Ps. lxix. 28</reference>. These judgments are called the <hi type="italic">burdens laid upon him</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.24.27">v. 27</reference>), for the wrath of God is a heavy burden, too heavy for any man to bear. Or it may be meant of the threatenings denounced against him by the prophets, for those are called <hi type="italic">burdens.</hi> Usually God sets some special marks of his displeasure upon apostates in this life, for warning to all to <hi type="italic">remember Lot's wife.</hi>  <chapter eID="2Chr.24"/> <div eID="gen8311" type="x-p"/>

Joash Reigns Well All the Days of Jehoiada.<div eID="gen5912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5913" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4083"/><hi type="bold">1-3. Joash ... began to reign--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.12.1-2Kgs.12.3">2Ki 12:1-3</reference>). <div eID="gen5913" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ab3cc7801d104829fe20e6227ee1edcafa88102: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4085"/><div sID="gen5915" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4085"/><hi type="bold">4-14. Joash was minded to repair the house of the Lord--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.12.4-2Kgs.12.16">2Ki 12:4-16</reference>).<div eID="gen5915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5916" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.15">2Ch 24:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.16">16</reference>. Jehoiada Being Dead. <div eID="gen5916" type="x-p"/>
entries.c2f4bb6b343d273d102e24a0fcca9de1dcd52f46: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4086"/><div sID="gen5917" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4086"/><hi type="bold">15-16. Jehoiada waxed old ... and died--</hi>His life, protracted to unusual longevity and spent in the service of his country, deserved some tribute of public gratitude, and this was rendered in the posthumous honors that were bestowed on him. Among the Hebrews, intramural interment was prohibited in every city but Jerusalem, and there the exception was made only to the royal family and persons of eminent merit, on whom the distinction was conferred of being buried in the city of David, among the kings, as in the case of Jehoiada.<div eID="gen5917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5918" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.17-2Chr.24.22">2Ch 24:17-22</reference>. Joash Falls into Idolatry. <div eID="gen5918" type="x-p"/>
entries.43b3b515fe10345c629d14003f47c01c7ec60886: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4087"/><div sID="gen5919" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4087"/><hi type="bold">17-22. Now came the princes of Judah, and make obeisance to the king--</hi>Hitherto, while Joash occupied the throne, his uncle had held the reins of sovereign power, and by his excellent counsels had directed the young king to such measures as were calculated to promote both the civil and religious interests of the country. The fervent piety, practical wisdom, and inflexible firmness of that sage counsellor exerted immense influence over all classes. But now that the helm of the state-ship was no longer steered by the sound head and firm hand of the venerable high priest, the real merits of Joash's administration appear; and for want of good and enlightened principle, as well as, perhaps, of natural energy of character, he allowed himself to be borne onward in a course which soon wrecked the vessel upon hidden rocks.<div eID="gen5919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5920" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the king hearkened unto them, &c.--</hi>They were secretly attached to idolatry, and their elevated rank affords sad proof how extensively and deeply the nation had become corrupted during the reigns of Jehoram, Ahaziah, and Athaliah. With strong professions of allegiance they humbly requested that they might not be subjected to the continued necessity of frequent and expensive journeys to Jerusalem, but allowed the privilege their fathers had enjoyed of worshipping God in high places at home. They framed their petition in this plausible and least offensive manner, well knowing that, if excused attendance at the temple, they might--without risk of discovery or disturbance--indulge their tastes in the observance of any private rites they pleased. The weak-minded king granted their petition; and the consequence was, that when they left the house of the Lord God of their fathers, they soon "served groves and idols." <div eID="gen5920" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6cd6fb8654e3db2fffe28245821779aab4eece3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4092"/><div sID="gen5928" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4092"/><hi type="bold">23. at the end of the year the host of Syria came up--</hi>This invasion took place under the personal conduct of Hazael, whom Joash, to save the miseries of a siege, prevailed on to withdraw his forces by a large present of gold (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.12.18">2Ki 12:18</reference>). Most probably, also, he promised the payment of an annual tribute, on the neglect or refusal of which the Syrians returned the following year, and with a mere handful of men inflicted a total and humiliating defeat on the collected force of the Hebrews. <div eID="gen5928" type="x-p"/>
entries.0a357eb98b8af1435b3eda03a3d66595a10f55f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4093"/><div sID="gen5929" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4093"/><hi type="bold">25. they left him in great diseases--</hi>The close of his life was embittered by a painful malady, which long confined him to bed.<div eID="gen5929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5930" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his own servants conspired against him--</hi>These two conspirators (whose fathers were Jews, but their mothers aliens) were probably courtiers, who, having constant access to the bedchamber, could the more easily execute their design.<div eID="gen5930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5931" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for the blood of the sons--</hi>read "the son" of Jehoiada. Public opinion seems to have ascribed the disasters of his life and reign to that foul crime. And as the king had long lost the esteem and respect of his subjects, neither horror nor sorrow was expressed for his miserable end! <chapter eID="2Chr.24"/>

entries.51462c82d78fc7e139bf5fa679acc84b4bea7420: <div eID="gen14433" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen14434" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14435" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14435" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14434" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14436" type="x-p"/> Joash begins to reign when seven years old, and reigns well all the days of Jehoiada the priest, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.1-2Chr.24.3">2Chr 24:1-3</reference>. He purposes to repair the temple of God; and makes a proclamation that the people should bring in the money prescribed by Moses, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.4-2Chr.24.9">2Chr 24:4-9</reference>. They all contribute liberally; and the different artificers soon perfect the work, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.10-2Chr.24.13">2Chr 24:10-13</reference>. The rest of the money is employed to form utensils for the temple, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.14">2Chr 24:14</reference>. Jehoiada dies, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.15">2Chr 24:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.16">2Chr 24:16</reference>. And the people after his death become idolaters, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.17">2Chr 24:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.18">2Chr 24:18</reference>. Prophets are sent unto them, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.19">2Chr 24:19</reference>. And among the rest Zechariah the son of Jehoiada, who testifies against them; and they stone him to death, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.20-2Chr.24.22">2Chr 24:20-22</reference>. The Syrians come against Jerusalem, and spoil it, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.23">2Chr 24:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.24">2Chr 24:24</reference>. Joash is murdered by his own servants, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.25">2Chr 24:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.26">2Chr 24:26</reference>. His acts, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.27">2Chr 24:27</reference>. <div eID="gen14436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14437" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen14437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14438" type="x-p"/> Joash was seven years old - As he was hidden six years in the temple, and was but seven when he came to the throne, he could have been but one year old when he was secreted by his aunt; see on <reference osisRef="2Chr.22.10">2Chr 22:10</reference> (note).
entries.e17433c18607bdcdfcfa371cdba17d83bfe6e9d4: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen14438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14439" type="x-p"/> To repair the house of the Lord - During the reigns of Joram and Athaliah, the temple of God had been pillaged to enrich that of Baal, and the whole structure permitted to fall into decay; see <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.7">2Chr 24:7</reference>.
entries.903cea44fd50cd1b1677bf3a62085104b068ce3f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen14439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14440" type="x-p"/> Gather of all Israel money - As the temple was the property of the whole nation, and the services performed in it were for the salvation of the people at large, it was right that each should come forward on an occasion of this kind, and lend a helping hand. This is the first instance of such a general collection for building or repairing a house of God. <div eID="gen14440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14441" type="x-p"/> From year to year - It must have been in a state of great dilapidation, when it required such annual exertions to bring it into a thorough state of repair.
entries.da1fe6fd68bd733cb6406b1e2613bc072eaa826e: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen14441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14442" type="x-p"/> The collection - of Moses - This was the poll-tax, fixed by Moses, of half a shekel, which was levied on every man from twenty years old and upward; and which was considered as a ransom for their souls, that there might be no plague among them. See <reference osisRef="Exo.30.12-Exo.30.14">Exo 30:12-14</reference>.
entries.ff5602a9b3431ffb96fc8b12847eb6819d3f4963: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen14442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14443" type="x-p"/> They made a chest - See the notes on the parallel places, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.12.4">2Kgs 12:4</reference> (note), etc.
entries.565163796279f900a9f644a3f39dae9a6ecfd78f: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen14443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14444" type="x-p"/> They buried him - among the kings - He had, in fact, been king in Judah; for Joash, who appears to have been a weak man, was always under his tutelage. Jehoiada governed the state in the name of the king; and his being buried among the kings is a proof of the high estimation in which he was held among the people.
entries.03057f88bcf46cf4abe70a6623dc1d39285fc55e: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen14444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14445" type="x-p"/> The princes of Judah - made obeisance to the king - I believe the Targum has given the true sense of this verse: "After the death of Jehoiada, the great men of Judah came and adored King Joash, and seduced him; and then the king received from them their idols."
entries.10daf73b316df227a797c8450c86e43088c60fb5: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen14445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14446" type="x-p"/> And the Spirit of God came upon Zechariah - "When he saw the transgression of the king and of the people, burning incense to an idol in the house of the sanctuary of the Lord, on the day of expiation; and preventing the priests of the Lord from offering the burnt-offerings, sacrifices, daily oblations, and services, as written in the book of the law of Moses; he stood above the people, and said." - Targum.
entries.8377102752dfcb8db444bec5f046dc81ae0aecd6: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen14446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14447" type="x-p"/> Stoned him - at the commandment of the king - What a most wretched and contemptible man was this, who could imbrue his hands in the blood of a prophet of God, and the son of the man who had saved him from being murdered, and raised him to the throne! Alas, alas! Can even kings forget benefits? But when a man falls from God, the devil enters into him; and then he is capable of every species of cruelty.
entries.93f27ab4165956454bfbff4a99114ea8104d2402: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen14447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14448" type="x-p"/> The Lord look upon it, and require it - And so he did; for, at the end of that year, the Syrians came against Judah, destroyed all the princes of the people, sent their spoils to Damascus; and Joash, the murderer of the prophet, the son of his benefactor, was himself murdered by his own servants. Here was a most signal display of the Divine retribution. <div eID="gen14448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14449" type="x-p"/> On the subject of the death of this prophet the reader is requested to refer to the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.23.34">Mat 23:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.23.35">Mat 23:35</reference>.
entries.b16b892f25bb2a9f762b29ce4a38d34823e9e8b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen14449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14450" type="x-p"/> These are they that conspired against him - The two persons here mentioned were certainly not Jews; the mother of one was an Ammonitess, and the mother of the other was a Moabitess. Who their fathers were we know not; they were probably foreigners and aliens. Some suppose that these persons were of the king's chamber, and therefore could have the easiest access to him. It has been, and is still, the folly of kings to have foreigners for their valets and most confidential servants, and they have often been the causes of murders and treacheries of different kinds. Foreigners should be banished from the person of the sovereign by strong and efficient laws: even in this country they have often been the cause of much political wo.
entries.0a770f924f88fb85355a4b339cc8bb245d0a466d: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen14450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14451" type="x-p"/> The greatness of the burdens laid upon him - Meaning, probably, the heavy tribute laid upon him by the Syrians; though some think the vast sums amassed for the repairs of the temple are here intended. <div eID="gen14451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14452" type="x-p"/> Written in the story - מדרש midrash, the commentary, of the book of Kings. We have met with this before; but these works are all lost, except the extracts found in Kings, Chronicles, and Ezra. These abridgments were the cause of the neglect, and finally of the destruction, of the originals. This has been often the case in works of great consequence. Trogus Pompeius wrote a general history of the world, which he brought down to the reign of Augustus, in forty-four volumes. Justin abridged them into one volume, and the original is lost.  <chapter eID="2Chr.24"/> <div eID="gen14452" type="x-p"/>

entries.8337443a8649f2325837e6ea9748368f2ce7b274: <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.1-2Chr.24.3">2Ch 24:1-3</reference> <hi type="italic">The reign of Joash;</hi> cf. 2 Kings 12. - In both accounts only two main events in Joash’s reign of forty years are narrated at any length, - the repair of the temple, and the campaign of the Syrian king Hazael against Jerusalem. Besides this, at the beginning, we have a statement as to the duration and spirit of his reign; and in conclusion, the murder of Joash in consequence of a conspiracy is mentioned. Both accounts agree in all essential points, but are shown to be extracts containing the most important part of a more complete history of Joash, by the fact that, on the one hand, in 2 Kings 12 single circumstances are communicated in a more detailed and more exact form than that in which the Chronicle states them; while, on the other hand, the account of the Chronicle supplements the account in 2 Kings 12 in many respects. To these latter belong the account of the marriage of Joash, and his many children, the account of the death of Jehoiada at the age of 130 years, and his honourable burial with the kings, etc.; see on 2Ch 24:15.
entries.a05e5cc441f1767514f9a148ee58d56cd508812d: <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.4-2Chr.24.10">2Ch 24:4-10</reference> <div eID="gen6100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6101" type="x-p"/> As to the <hi type="italic">repair of the temple</hi>, see the commentary on 2Ki 12:5-17, where both the formal divergences and the essential agreement of the two narratives are pointed out.
entries.401015ff33f2555990542a089817ce514d809bdf: <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.11-2Chr.24.12">2Ch 24:11-12</reference> וגו יביא בּעת ויהי, translate: It came to pass at the time when they brought the chest to the guard of the king by the Levites, i.e., to the board of oversight appointed by the king from among the Levites. עת <hi type="italic">stat. constr.</hi> before a sentence following. בּכום ליום does not denote every day, but every time when there was much money in the chest.
entries.e3a4c41aae875bb47d96c8fb86d85284746ecd0b: <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.13">2Ch 24:13</reference> ארוּכה ותּעל, and there was a band laid upon the work, i.e., the restoration of the house of God was furthered; cf. for this symbolical expression, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.1">Neh 4:1</reference>; Jer 8:7.
entries.d56281ab0aa93958b63b3806e46d9de051ead20d: <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.14">2Ch 24:14</reference> כּלים ויּעשׂהוּ, therefrom (the king) caused to be made (prepared) vessels for the house of Jahve, (namely) vessels of the service, i.e., according to Num 4:12, in the holy place, and for the offering of burnt-offering, i.e., altar vessels, and (besides) bowls, and (other) vessels of gold and silver. The last clause of <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.14">2Ch 24:14</reference> leads on to the following: “They (king and people) offered burnt-offering continually so long as Jehoiada lived.”
entries.5481ddc99f027b259c8e850c00fd6f1dbc5fc55d: <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.15-2Chr.24.16">2Ch 24:15-16</reference> <hi type="italic">Jehoiada’s death: the fall of the people into idolatry: the protest of the prophet Zechariah against it, and the stoning of him</hi>. - This section is not found in 2 Kings 12, but is important for the understanding of the later history of Joash (2Ch 24:23.). With the death of the grey-haired high priest came a turning-point in the reign of Joash. Jehoiada had saved the life and throne of Joash, preserved to the kingdom the royal house of David, to which the promises belonged, and had put an end to the idolatry which had been transplanted into Judah by Joram’s marriage into the royal house of Ahab, restoring the Jahve-worship. For this he was honoured at his death, his body being laid in the city of David among the kings: “For he had done good in Israel, and towards God and His house” (the temple). According to 2Ki 12:7, he still took an active part in the repair of the temple in the twenty-third year of Joash, and according to <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.14">2Ch 24:14</reference> he lived for some time after the completion of that work. But after his death the people soon forgot the benefits they owed him.
entries.72c6c895fbab9dcf594bf532e1919ac0f0adde1c: <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.17-2Chr.24.20">2Ch 24:17-20</reference> <div eID="gen6101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6102" type="x-p"/> The princes of Judah besought the king to allow them to worship the Astartes and idols, and the king hearkened to them, did not venture to deny their request. למּלך ישׁתּחווּ, they bowed themselves before the king, i.e., they besought him. What they thus beseechingly requested is not stated, but may be gathered from what they did, according to 2Ch 24:18. They forsook Jahve the God of their fathers, etc. There came wrath upon Judah because of this their trespass. קצף, a wrathful judgment of the Lord, cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.8">2Ch 29:8</reference>, viz., the invasion of the land by Hazael, 2Ch 24:23. On the construction זאת אשׁמתם, cf. Ew. §293, <hi type="italic">c</hi>, S. 740. Against this defection prophets whom the Lord sent did indeed lift up their testimony, but they would not hearken to them. Of these prophets, one, Zechariah the son of the high priest Jehoiada, is mentioned by name in 2Ch 24:20., who, seized by the Spirit of the Lord, announced to the people divine punishment for their defection, and was thereupon, at the king’s command, stoned in the court of the temple. With לבשׁה רוּח cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.18">1Ch 12:18</reference>, and the commentary on Jdg 6:34. לעם מעל, above the people, viz., as we learn from <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.21">2Ch 24:21</reference>, in the inner, higher-lying court, so that he was above the people who were in the outer court. “Why transgress ye the commandments of the Lord, and (why) will ye not prosper?” Fidelity to the Lord is the condition of prosperity. If Israel forsake the Lord, the Lord will also forsake it; cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.5">2Ch 12:5</reference>; 2Ch 15:2.
entries.634c9212fdd14bb2a7ee373795da024a171858b0: <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.21-2Chr.24.22">2Ch 24:21-22</reference> <div eID="gen6102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6103" type="x-p"/> And they (the princes and the people) conspired against him, and stoned him, at the command of the king, in the court of the temple. This זכריה is the Ζαχαρίας whose slaughter is mentioned by Christ in <reference osisRef="Matt.23.36">Mat 23:36</reference> and <reference osisRef="Luke.11.51">Luk 11:51</reference> as the last prophet-murder narrated in the Old Testament, whose blood would come upon the people, although Matthew calls him υἱὸς Βαραχίου. According to these passages, he was slain between the temple and the altar of burnt-offering, consequently in the most sacred part of the court of the priests. That the king, Joash, could give the command for this murder, shows how his compliance with the princes’ demands (<reference osisRef="2Chr.24.17">2Ch 24:17</reference>) had made him the slave of sin. Probably the idolatrous princes accused the witness for God of being a seditious person and a rebel against the majesty of the crown, and thereby extorted from the weak king the command for his death. For it is not said that Joash himself worshipped the idols; and even in <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.22">2Ch 24:22</reference> it is only the base ingratitude of which Joash had been guilty, in the slaughter of the son of his benefactor, which is adduced against him. But Zechariah at his death said, “May the Lord look upon it, and take vengeance” (דּרשׁ, to seek or require a crime, i.e., punish it). This word became a prophecy, which soon began to be fulfilled, 2Ch 24:23.
entries.8b23c04700fb3a07b756c71dbec15934ae6900ef: <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.23-2Chr.24.27">2Ch 24:23-27</reference> <div eID="gen6103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6104" type="x-p"/> The punishment comes upon them. <hi type="italic">Joash afflicted by the invasion of Judah by Hazael the Syrian; and his death in consequence of a conspiracy against him</hi>. - These two events are narrated in 2Ki 12:18-21 also, the progress of Hazael’s invasion being more exactly traced; see the commentary on 2Ki 12:18. The author of the Chronicle brings forward only those parts of it which show how God punished Joash for his defection from Him. <div eID="gen6104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6105" type="x-p"/> “At the revolution of a year,” i.e., scarcely a year after the murder of the prophet Zechariah, a Syrian army invaded Judah and advanced upon Jerusalem; “and they destroyed all the princes of the people from among the people,” i.e., they smote the army of Joash in a battle, in which the princes (the chief and leaders) were destroyed, i.e., partly slain, partly wounded. This punishment came upon the princes as the originators of the defection from the Lord, 2Ch 24:17. “And they sent all their booty to the king (Hazael) to Damascus.” In this booty the treasures which Joash gave to the Syrians (2Ki 12:19) to buy their withdrawal are also included. In order to show that this invasion of the Syrians was a divine judgment, it is remarked in <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.24">2Ch 24:24</reference> that the Syrians, with a small army, gained a victory over the very large army of Judah, and executed judgment upon Joash. שׁפטים עשׂה, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.12.12">Exo 12:12</reference>; Num 33:4, frequently in Ezekiel, usually construed with בּ, here with את, analogous to the את טּוב עשׂה, e.g., 1Sa 24:19. These words refer to the wounding of Joash, and its results, 2Ch 24:25. In the war Joash was badly wounded; the Syrians on their withdrawal had left him behind in many wounds (מחליים only met with here, synonymous with תּחלאים,   <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.19">2Ch 21:19</reference>). Then his own servants, the court officials named in <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.26">2Ch 24:26</reference>, conspired against him, and smote him upon his bed. In 2Ki 12:21, the place where the king, lying sick upon his bed, was slain is stated. He met with his end thus, “because of the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest” which had been shed. The plural בּני is perhaps only an orthographical error for בּן, occasioned by the preceding דּמי (Berth.); but more probably it is, like בּנין,   <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.3">2Ch 28:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Chr.33.6">2Ch 33:6</reference>, a rhetorical plural, which says nothing as to the number, but only brings out that Joash had brought blood-guiltiness upon himself in respect of the children of his benefactor Jehoiada; see on 2Ch 28:3. Upon the murdered king, moreover, the honour of being buried in the graves of the kings was not bestowed; cf. 2Ch 21:20. On the names of the two conspirators, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.26">2Ch 24:26</reference>, see on 2Ki 12:21. In <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.27">2Ch 24:27</reference> it is doubtful how ורב is to be read. The <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> demands ירב, which Berth. understands thus: And as regards his sons, may the utterance concerning him increase; which might signify, “May the wish of the dying Zechariah, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.22">2Ch 24:22</reference>, be fulfilled on them in a still greater degree than on their father.” But that is hardly the meaning of the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>. The older theologians took ירב relatively: <hi type="italic">et quam creverit s. multiplicatum fuerit</hi>. Without doubt, the Keth. ורב or ורב is the correct reading. המּשּׂא, too, is variously interpreted. Vulg., Luther, and others take it to be synonymous with משׂאת, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.6">2Ch 24:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.9">2Ch 24:9</reference>, and understand it of the money derived from Moses’ tax; but to that עליו is by no means suitable. Others (as Then.) think of the tribute laid upon him, 2Ki 12:19, but very arbitrarily. On the other hand, Clericus and others rightly understand it of prophetic threatenings against him, corresponding to the statement in <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.19">2Ch 24:19</reference>, that God sent prophets against him. As to the Midrash of the book of Kings, see the Introduction.  <chapter eID="2Chr.24"/> <div eID="gen6105" type="x-p"/>
